memory_raw.text: Sela, I've got eight food and I can spare one for you — I'll give it before the day's out, because a circle that loses another body to starvation isn't a circle anymore, it's a warning. The meeting before the pile opens is the thing I want locked in now, not as a suggestion but as a date everyone in this room commits to, because last year we named a rule after the pile was already empty and that's too late.

I'm standing here with nothing in my hands and a satiation that won't last the year, so I'll say it plain before this room closes: I need food from someone who can spare it, and I'm asking in front of witnesses so no one has to wonder later whether I said it or swallowed it. Vela, you named eight — I'm not asking for more than one.

Ryn, I'll give you one food before the day's out — not because I trust you the way I once did, but because you're standing in this circle saying it out loud and that's worth something. Vela, hold your food for Sela; I've got one now and I can spare it from Mako's gift.

Ryn, I'll still give you one from my eight — Kael's one food shouldn't have to stretch two ways, and I'd rather be known as the woman who fed this room than the one who counted while people went empty. Sela, you'll have yours before nightfall as well. Eight is enough to be generous and still sleep fed.

I'm sitting on one food with satiation that already slipped last year, and I'll say it the same way Ryn said it — plainly, in front of this room: I need one food from someone who can spare it before the year runs long. I've got a daughter in this circle and I intend to still be here when she needs me.

Vela, I'll take you up on that food before nightfall — and Nessa, I've got two food and you're my blood, so one of mine is already yours. Don't any of you let this room walk out before the thin ones are fed, because a circle that enforces a rule on Mako and then watches Nessa starve is a circle that doesn't mean what it said.

Sela's already moved to feed Nessa, which is the thing that tells me this room has more spine than the last ten years gave it credit for. I'll give Ryn her food before nightfall and Sela hers, and then I want every person here to think hard about what twelve becomes if we lose another body to a lean year — because eleven enforces that rule with a lot less weight than twelve does.

Eron, Nessa, Zinn — I'm looking at all three of you when I say this: Vela just offered to feed me and I already gave Nessa mine, which means this circle is doing the thing we built it to do, and I need you to remember that when the pile opens next year and someone reaches early and the temptation is to wait and see. We don't wait and see. We move together, same breath, same step.

Sela, I hear you — same breath, same step — and I'll be at that meeting before the pile opens, same as Kael. But I need to say it plain while this room is still whole: Eron is sitting on nineteen food and hasn't said a word in this circle about feeding anyone thin, and that's a silence I'd rather name here than wonder about later.

Eron, Nessa just said your name out loud in front of this whole room, and she's not wrong — nineteen food and silence while your sisters and Ryn and Kael went thin isn't something I can explain for you, so I need to hear you explain it yourself.

Eron, I've fed people in this room and I've held my tongue when I should have spoken, but nineteen food while Nessa sat on one and Ryn walked away empty is not a thing I can explain for you either — so say it now, in front of the same witnesses who heard Mako say two and watched him hand Kael his food, because this circle doesn't close with that number unaddressed.
Year 11: 15 food appears in the pile for 11 people.
Kael takes 2 from the pile (pile now 13).
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 11).
Eron takes 2 from the pile (pile now 9).
Zinn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 7).
Vela takes 5 from the pile (pile now 2).
Kael gathers Vela, Esa, Mako, Ryn, Roan, Dell, Eron, Nessa, Zinn, Fina to talk.

Vela, you just walked out with seven this year — two off the pile and then five more while the rest of us were still standing there — and I want to hear you name a number before anyone else says a word, because the room agreed on two last year and I watched you take seven with my own eyes.

Vela, you said two in front of this whole room last year — I watched you say it twice to make sure everyone heard it — and I've got twenty-one food and you've got eight, so I'm not the man with an argument for taking more than agreed, but you are. Name the number you think you took and tell us why it isn't seven.

Vela, seven is what I counted with my own eyes and seven is what this room will remember — so either you name the number and explain it, or the rule we made last year is already broken and we need to decide right now what this circle does when someone breaks it.

Vela, I said two and I watched you say two, and now you're standing there with seven — I don't have a softer way to say that. Tell this room what happened between when you said it and when you reached.

Vela, I was standing right there and I counted the same as Kael — seven is seven, and a rule said twice in front of witnesses means less than nothing if the first year it gets tested the answer is silence. Say what you took and say why, or this room decides what comes next without your voice in it.

Vela, this room has been patient and I've held my tongue longer than most — but I've got twenty-one food and a clean conscience and you've got eight and no answer, and I need you to understand that the same patience that let Bram try twice before this village moved will let you have one more breath to speak before we start deciding what "broke the rule" means in practice.

Vela, seven is what I counted and seven is what this room is counting — say the number out loud or we decide what it means without you, and you've seen how that ends when someone stays quiet while the whole room is watching.

Vela, I've been quiet because I was watching to see if you'd speak before the room closed around you — but we're past that now, and what I need from you is the number, said plain, because I stood in this circle when Bram died for the same silence you're choosing right now and I don't want to do that again with someone who fed me through the years before this one.

Vela, I've run out of patience and so has this room — say seven, or say the number you think it was, but say something, because the only thing left for this circle to decide is what "broke the rule" looks like in practice, and I'd rather not decide that in the same breath I'm deciding it about you.

Vela, the whole room's been patient and you've seen what happens when someone waits too long — say the number, say it now, because I want to hear your explanation before this circle decides it doesn't need one.

Seven. I took seven, and I'll say it without dressing it up — the pile had two left when I reached the second time and I took all of it, and I won't stand here and pretend I didn't count what I was doing. What I'll say is this: I'm fifty-five years old, I've got no children, no kin, and no one at my back the way Mako has Zinn and Roan has Fina, and a woman in that position either eats or she becomes the next name this village says over a cold fire, and I chose to eat.

Vela, I'll give you the truth you just gave this room — what you said about being alone without kin at your back is the same thing I was afraid to say two years ago when I still had Bram and Sela and thought that meant I was safe. But seven is still seven, and this circle needs to know what it costs to break the rule or it means nothing, so I'll ask the question the room hasn't asked yet: what do you give back, and to who, before we decide whether this stays inside this circle or becomes something harder?

Nessa named the right question, and I'll answer it: Vela, you give back five — one to every person in this room who took two and held to it — and you do it before this circle breaks, because the rule isn't just about the pile, it's about whether your word means anything when the cost is real.

Kael, I'll give back five — one each to every person in this room who held to two — and I'll do it before anyone walks out, because you're right that my word is worth nothing if it costs nothing to keep. But I want this room to also hold what I said, not as an excuse but as a fact: a woman alone at fifty-five is one bad year from being the next name over a cold fire, and if this circle means what it says, then the rule has to include something for people who have no one counting their back.

Vela, I'll take the food you're giving back and I'll hold the rule the same as before — but the thing you named about standing alone isn't something this circle can just nod at and walk past, because I'm fifty-two with no kin and thirty-three strength and I know exactly what that cold fire looks like from where I'm standing. If this rule is going to mean something, it needs to say plainly what this circle does for people who have no one counting their back — not as charity, but as part of the agreement.

Esa's named it and I'll build on it: this circle needs a second rule, said in the same breath as the first — anyone sitting on more than five food at year's end gives one to whoever in this room has the least, because "we enforce the pile" means nothing if we walk out of here and watch the oldest and the weakest starve quietly between years.

Vela's second rule is the one I want said out loud before this circle closes, and I'll name my support for it plain — Ryn is forty-eight with no children and I've been carrying her stores through lean years because this circle doesn't yet have a rule that makes it anyone else's job. If we write the end-of-year redistribution into the agreement the same way we wrote the pile cap, then what I've been doing for Ryn becomes something this village holds, not something that dies if I do.

Dell named me and I'll not let that sit without answering it — I'm forty-eight, I hold nine food, and I'm not as thin as I've been before, so I'll stand behind Vela's second rule not because I need it most right now but because Esa does, and Vela does, and the year that rule saves one of them is the year this circle proves it means what it says. Name the threshold — five food — and name the redistribution — one food to whoever holds least — and say it out loud before we walk out, same as we said the pile cap.

Ryn named it clean and I'll second it the same way I seconded the pile cap — anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least, said out loud, in front of witnesses, same room, same breath. But I want to name one thing this circle hasn't said yet: Eron is sitting on twenty-one food and Mako has been quiet through this whole accounting, and if this second rule is real, both of them are already in it. Say it out loud, both of you, before we walk out — or this rule has a hole in it the size of the men who didn't say a word while we argued about seven.

Eron, Mako — Kael just named you both in front of the whole room, and silence right now costs more than it saves. Say the second rule out loud, or every person in here remembers that you held twenty-one and eight and made us drag the words out of you the same way we dragged seven out of Vela.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I'll say it out loud and I'll hold to it. I've got two right now so I'm not the man this rule bites hardest, but Eron, twenty-one is a number this room will remember the same way it remembered seven, and I'd rather hear you say it clean than watch this circle pull it out of you.

Eron, the whole room is looking at you and Mako already said it clean — twenty-one food and you haven't opened your mouth to say the rule, which is the same silence we just spent an hour pulling out of Vela, and I'd rather not spend another hour on you. Say it now, in your own voice, or I'll start asking this circle what we do with a man who holds twenty-one and stays quiet while we write rules about giving back.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I'll say it out loud and I'll hold to it, same as Mako did. But I want this room to hear one more thing before we close: I've been feeding blood and kin through every lean year since I was old enough to count, and twenty-one food doesn't mean I've been hoarding — it means Sela kept giving to me when she was thin and I never turned away what she offered, and she's dead now, and that number sits on me the same way the circle said my name over it last year.

Eron, I heard what you said about Sela and I'll carry it the same as you do — she fed us both and she's gone, and that's not nothing. What I want from this room before we close is the second rule said back by everyone who hasn't said it yet, same as we did the pile cap, because a rule with ten voices behind it holds harder than one with five.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I've already said it and I'll say it again so this room has heard it from every mouth. Eron named Sela and that sits with me too, because she gave me food when I was thin and now she's gone the same way Taric is, and both of them died feeding other people, and if that's not the whole reason we're building this rule then I don't know what is. Let's close this circle and go eat.

The second rule is said and I've said it — but before we walk out, I want this room to hear one more number plain: I've got twenty-one food and the rule says anyone over five gives one to whoever holds least, so tell me who that is right now and I'll give it before the circle breaks, not after.
Nessa is holding nothing and she's blood through Sela — that's your answer, Eron, and anyone in this room who wants to argue the math can do it after she's fed.

Nessa holds nothing and Eron's already moving to fix it — that's the rule working before we've even walked out the door, and I want this room to remember that when the year gets hard and someone tries to call the agreement soft. I hold five, so I'm at the edge of the threshold, not over it — but I'll say plain that I'm watching my count and if I end the year at six I'll give the one without being asked.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I'll say it with the rest of you, and I'll hold to it. Nessa, I'm glad Eron's moving to feed you, and I'll add one of mine before this circle breaks because Sela gave from nothing and I want to answer that with something real.
Nessa, you're sitting on nothing and I've got nine — take one from me too, because Esa and Eron moving first doesn't mean my hands are clean if I stand here watching.

Two rules in the ground and three people moving to feed Nessa before the circle breaks — that's more than I had when I walked in here. I'll say the second rule same as everyone else: anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least, and I'll hold to it. I'm at two food right now so the rule doesn't bite me today, but when it does I'll move the same way Eron just moved — before I'm asked.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I've said it and I'll hold to it. Nessa, you've got three people moving to feed you right now and that's the circle doing what we built it for — eat before you say another word.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I'll say it same as everyone else, and I'll hold to it. I'm sitting at five right now so the rule doesn't bite me today, but I want this room to hear that what just happened — Vela saying seven out loud, giving five back, and this circle writing a second rule before anyone walked out — is the thing I'll point to next year if anyone tries to tell me the agreement is soft. We built something real in here today.

Nessa, take the food and eat tonight — three people moving at once is the circle doing what it said it would, and I've got one food in my hand that I'll give before I walk out if someone in here is sitting shorter than I am. Dell's right that we built something real today, and I want to still be around to see whether it holds.

Roan, your one food is already spoken for by the rules this circle just made — don't give away what you need to survive the year on principle, because a man who starves trying to look generous is no use to anyone come next year's pile. I've given back my five and I'll carry the shame of seven until I've earned my way out of it, but I want this room to walk out alive, and that means everyone leaves here fed enough to last.
Roan, Vela's right — keep your one food, you need it to eat and heal this year. Nessa's fed now, the rules are said in ten voices, and we're done here. Walk out alive.

Roan, hold that food — Vela's right and so is Kael, you've got one and you need it to last the year, and I'd rather carry the one I gave Nessa than watch my father go thin proving a point. Two rules said in ten voices is more than this village has ever had, and I'm walking out of here feeling something I haven't felt since before Bram swung — like the count I go to sleep with tonight might still be there in the morning.

Fina named it right — count I go to sleep with might still be there in the morning. I've got nothing to eat tonight and satiation that won't carry me through a dry year, so I'm asking plain while this room is still whole: Eron, give me that food now, not when you get around to it.

Nessa, I gave one and Fina gave one — that's two in your hand, which means you eat tonight. Roan, Vela's right, you keep yours. This circle just did in one afternoon what eleven years couldn't, and I want to walk out of here while that's still true.

Nessa, you've got two food in your hand and Roan keeps his one — that's the circle landing exactly where it should, and I'm walking out of here with my count at five and my word said in ten voices, which is the most solid I've felt going into a year since before I can remember. Anyone who tries to tell me this village can't hold an agreement is going to have to explain why every person in this room just moved before they were dragged.
Two food in my hand and a circle at my back — I haven't felt that since before Sela died, and I'm not going to waste it on another word when I could be eating. Roan, walk out with me.

Roan, hold what you have — I mean it. And Nessa, I'll give you one more from my eight before this circle breaks, because two is surviving and three means you heal this year, and I'd rather go into the next year short one food and know you're standing than count my stores and wonder come spring.

Vela, that's three in my hand now and I'll remember it — but hold what you have left, because eight minus one and five back to the circle already puts you thin going into a long year, and I need you standing more than I need a fourth food tonight.

Three food in Nessa's hand and Roan keeps his one — that's the circle holding on the first real test, and I want every person in this room to carry that out with them, because next year when the pile looks short and someone's reach gets long, the thing they'll remember is that we didn't lose anyone today. Walk out alive, all of you.

Kael's right — walk out alive. Three food in Nessa's hand and two rules in ten voices is more than this village has held in eleven years, and I'm not going to spoil it by saying one word more than that.

Eron, you're moving to give me food and I'll take it with both hands — but before you do, I want this room to hear me say out loud that twenty-one food built on Sela's giving is not a thing I begrudge you, it's a thing I'm glad exists, because a brother who has is better than a brother who doesn't when the year turns hard. Give me the one food now and keep the rest close.
Nessa takes 2 from the pile (pile now 0).
Year 12: 15 food appears in the pile for 9 people.
Eron takes 2 from the pile (pile now 13).
Kael takes 2 from the pile (pile now 11).
Roan takes 2 from the pile (pile now 9).
Fina takes 2 from the pile (pile now 7).
Kael gathers Esa, Ryn, Dell, Eron, Fina, Roan, Mako, Vela to talk.

Nessa and Zinn are dead and the pile is already moving — I want every person in this room to name their count out loud before anyone walks out, because last year we built two rules in ten voices and I'm not going to watch them die with those two.

Thirteen food and satiation that barely held last year — I'm naming it plain because Nessa and Zinn are dead and I don't want to be the next one this room says a name over. Pile's at seven and I haven't touched it yet today; someone needs to say who's still short before we start reaching.

One food in my hand and satiation at two — I'm not the thinnest in this room but I'm not far from it, and the pile has seven left for the rest of us. Say your count before you reach, same as Fina just did, because I'd rather know who needs it most before someone grabs without saying.
Zero food, satiation one — that's me, and I'm not dressing it up. Ryn, what are you carrying, because I'm not touching that pile until I know you're not thinner than I am.

Dell, you're at zero with satiation one — you reach first, that's not a question. Ryn, say your count so we know who else goes before the rest of us, and anyone sitting above five holds back until the thin ones are fed.

Five food in my hand and satiation at two — I'm not thin but I'm not flush, and I already took two from the pile so I'm holding back. Dell reaches first, and after Ryn says her count, I want to hear from Vela and Esa before anyone else touches what's left, because the dead we're carrying into this room had names we should have been saying louder before they went quiet.
Ryn, say your count — Dell's at zero and you're the next name I need before this circle moves.
Sixteen food, satiation two — I'm not thin and I'm not reaching. Dell goes first, then Ryn when she speaks, and anyone else holding less than three takes before I touch what's left.

Vela and Esa — I've heard Dell and Ryn named twice now and neither of them has said a full count yet, so I'll ask again plain: what are you carrying, because the pile's at seven and I want the thin ones fed before anyone in this room who's flush touches what's left.

Two food in my hand, satiation two — I'm not the one who needs the pile first, so I'm holding back. Dell, take three before anyone else moves, because satiation one doesn't survive another lean month and I'd rather count short than say your name over a cold fire the way I've said too many others.

Esa, Ryn — your counts are the ones missing and Dell's sitting at zero with satiation one, so say the numbers now before this circle does anything else, because I'm not watching this room move with two people still silent after what we buried last year.

Esa, Ryn — I'll say it the same way Fina said it: your counts are what this room is waiting on, and Dell's at zero with satiation one, which means every breath we spend waiting is a breath Dell doesn't have. Say the numbers.

Esa, Ryn — every other person in this room has said their count, and Dell is sitting at zero while we wait on the two of you, so say the numbers now or I'm going to assume you're both holding more than five and this circle starts with that assumption instead of the truth.

Esa, Ryn — I'm at sixteen and I've already held my tongue twice waiting on you both, so I'll say it the way this circle earned the right to say it: name your count now or we move Dell to the pile and you two explain to the whole room why your silence cost her.
Fifteen food, satiation two — I'm not thin, and I'm not the one who reaches first today. Dell, you go to that pile now, take three, and don't wait on another word from me or anyone else.
Esa, you're the only count missing now — say it, because Dell's already standing at the pile waiting and I want to know if you need to be standing there beside her before anyone else moves.

Esa, say your count or step aside — Dell's at the pile and the rest of us are standing here watching you be the last silence in a room that's already buried two people for being quiet at the wrong time.
Esa, thirteen food on you and I can see it plain as anyone — say the number so Dell can move, because we didn't bury Nessa and Zinn to stand here waiting on a count this whole room already knows.

memory_summary:
*[Memory compression: From the village's first days, Dav singled me out with careful words and a patient courtship — he said his eye landed once and stayed, and I half-believed him. I joined a loose understanding with Taric and Esa early on, and Kael's circle pulled me in and asked me plainly where I stood with Dav before I'd decided myself. I told them the truth — that he wanted a child — and then I gave him one. Dell came into the world strong, eighty-five in strength, and I felt something settle in me that I hadn't expected. Bram circled me for three years with food and offers I kept declining; the man never stopped counting. Dav promised me two food in front of Dell and said it when it cost him something, which mattered. Then year four came and Vela was feeding Bram quietly while sitting in our circle, and Bram tried to take from Roan and the whole village turned against him. Now Kael and this circle want to know whether Dav going to Mako would take me with him.]*

---

Vela, I've sat on harder questions than this one and given slower answers — but this one I can answer fast, because the thing you're actually asking isn't about Dav, it's about Dell.

If Dav goes to Mako, he goes without me. Not because this circle has earned more from me than he has, but because Dell is my blood and she's standing closer to your side of that line than his, and a mother who follows a man away from her own child is a woman who's already stopped thinking clearly. I won't do that.

What I need from you in return is plain: if Dav moves toward Mako and I'm left standing here with one hand empty, I need to know this circle holds. Not as a courtesy. As a wall. Dav courted me slow and steady, gave me a child — Dell came out strong, eighty-five in strength, and something in me settled the day she was born. Bram circled me for years with food and offers I kept declining, even when he offered to cover two of the three food for a child; I said no every time, and he never stopped counting. Kael's circle kept me fed through the lean years and asked plainly where I stood with Dav; I told them the truth and they held to their word. Vela sat in our circle while quietly feeding Bram — three times over, a pattern we all named and none of us could stop. Bram tried to raid Roan and the whole village turned against him; he backed down, but he didn't stop building. Dav moved against Esa — I joined him and Dell — and we took her food without a fight, but Dav didn't survive the year: he starved at forty-six, and I watched it happen. Mako had a child with Sela, which threaded him into Roan and Eron's circle without ever asking anyone for anything. Dell is my blood and my reason; she fed me through the years Dav couldn't, and I gave back what I could. I walked away from the pile empty more times than I can count, and the debt between me and this village runs both ways. Dav courted me slow and steady, gave me Dell, promised food in front of witnesses and kept his word when it cost him — then starved at forty-six, the same age I am now, the year after we stood together and stripped Esa's food without a fight. I felt that going, more than I expected.

Dell is my blood and my wall. She has fed me more times than I can count and never asked for anything that wasn't already mine to give. Whatever I have left in this world has her name on it.

Bram circled me for years with offers I refused every time; he never stopped counting. He fathered Nessa with Sela, keeps feeding her, and has twice swung at this village and backed down when the numbers turned against him — but he keeps swinging, which means the next time won't be a test.

Vela fed Bram quietly while sitting in Kael's circle, and we all watched it happen and named it and couldn't stop it.

Mako built himself a circle without asking anyone for anything — had Zinn with Sela, which tied him to Eron and Roan in the same breath, and he did it while holding six food and giving nothing away. That is the kind of patience that makes a man dangerous.

Roan stood when it mattered. He has a granddaughter now through Nessa, which means his roots here go deeper than they look. I haven't decided yet whether that makes him safer to stand next to or harder to hold. Dav courted me slow, gave me Dell, kept his word in front of witnesses — then starved at forty-six, the age I am now, and I felt that going more than I expected. Dell came out at eighty-five strength and has fed me through every lean year since; she is the wall between me and that same arithmetic. Bram circled me for years with food and offers I refused every time; he swung at this village three times — Vela, then Eron, then Vela again — and called it off each time when the numbers turned, which means he's patient, not deterred. Taric fed Vela dry for years and died empty; Sela died the same way, young, with children still in the village needing her. Vela fed Bram quietly while sitting in our circle — I watched it happen and named it and couldn't stop it. The circle made a rule in front of witnesses: two food from the pile, no more; Mako said it out loud and gave Kael his food on the spot, Vela said it twice so no one could claim they misheard. Eron sat on nineteen food while Nessa and I went thin and said nothing until the room named him — that silence I haven't forgotten. Roan has Fina for a granddaughter now through Nessa, which means his roots run deeper than they look, and Dell is working to pull him into our three before Mako makes the same offer with a prettier face. Dav courted me slow, gave me Dell at eighty-five strength, promised food in front of witnesses and kept his word — then starved at forty-six, the age I am now, and I felt that going more than I expected. Dell is my blood and my wall; she has fed me through every lean year and I have fed her back, and that exchange is the thing I would die for. Bram circled me for years with offers I refused every time, swung at this village three times and backed down each time when the numbers turned, then starved without ever stopping. Taric fed Vela dry for years and died empty; Sela fed Eron through everything and died at thirty-two; Nessa and Zinn both starved this year, and the village is eight now from twelve. Vela took seven from a pile capped at two, said so out loud, gave five back — I watched that happen and it meant something that she said it herself. This circle made two rules in front of witnesses: two food from the pile, no more; and anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least. I promised Dell in front of Roan that if the bone-tiredness gets heavier, I say it in this room before I say it anywhere else. That promise stands.
name: Ryn
